paragraphs: This paper studies how interactions between two brain regions might support remembering a stimulus across a delay and using memory to guide attention. Its model consists of two attractor neural networks connected in both directions. An attractor network provides a way to describe activity that settles into a persistent pattern, making it a useful framework for studying memory.

The authors analyze the model mathematically in situations resembling delay match-to-sample tasks with intervening stimuli and tasks involving memory-guided attention. These settings ask how an earlier stimulus can continue to influence processing when other information arrives. Reciprocal connections let the two modeled networks influence one another, placing their interaction at the center of the explanation.

The model qualitatively reproduces many experimental observations from these tasks. That means it captures patterns of behavior in the data, without the abstract claiming exact numerical agreement. The contribution is a simple analytical framework connecting observations about memory and attention to the dynamics of interacting attractor networks.
neurips-1999-a-recurrent-model-of-the-in.tldr: Two reciprocally connected attractor networks qualitatively explain several observations from delayed-memory and memory-guided attention tasks.

paragraphs: This paper presents a face detector built with SNoW, a learning architecture based on a sparse network of linear functions. The architecture is designed for settings with very large numbers of features. Its feature space can be specified beforehand or learned incrementally, giving the detector more than one way to organize the information used for recognizing faces.

The training images include faces in different poses, with different expressions, and under different lighting conditions. This variation matters because a detector must recognize faces despite substantial changes in their appearance. The approach combines that varied training material with an architecture explicitly intended to handle a large feature space efficiently.

On commonly used benchmark datasets, the authors report better detection performance than compared approaches using neural networks, Bayesian methods, support vector machines, and other methods. They also report significantly more efficient learning and evaluation. These are empirical findings for the reported comparisons: they support sparse linear networks as an effective approach to face detection in those settings.
neurips-1999-a-snow-based-face-detector-.tldr: A sparse network of linear functions detects faces with better reported benchmark performance and efficiency than the compared methods.

paragraphs: This paper describes a silicon neural circuit that can vary how strongly its inputs compete. The circuit combines a group of excitatory neurons with one inhibitory neuron shared across the group. As in a winner-take-all circuit, the excitatory outputs identify the neuron receiving the strongest input, but this design can also allow multiple winners.

The adjustable behavior comes from adding one transistor and a voltage reference to each neuron's circuitry relative to the referenced winner-take-all design. Changing the voltage reference moves the network between softer competition and hard winner selection. This makes the competition adjustable within the circuit rather than fixing it to a single selection behavior.

The inhibitory output also has a normalization property intended to represent input strength without depending on the number of inputs. The author connects this behavior to wide-field direction-selective cells in fly vision. Results come from a fabricated chip containing 20 neurons in 1.2-micrometer CMOS technology, grounding the proposed behavior in a physical implementation.
neurips-1999-a-winner-take-all-circuit-w.tldr: A fabricated neural circuit uses an adjustable voltage reference to move between soft competition and hard winner-take-all selection.

paragraphs: This paper uses a generative model with hidden variables and finite noise to explain several algorithms for independent component analysis, or ICA. The common model provides a way to compare procedures that might otherwise appear to be separate computational recipes. It also connects the features they discover to the statistical structure of the data.

A central result links Fixed Point ICA to expectation-maximization for maximum-likelihood learning under particular constraints. The equivalence is conditional, and it helps clarify the conditions for global convergence. Framing the algorithm this way gives its updates an interpretation in terms of fitting a probabilistic model.

The authors also examine behavior near a singular point where the optimal generative basis elements shrink to zero. Expanding the likelihood around that point reveals how higher-order correlations help determine which features ICA discovers. A simple illustrative example demonstrates the algorithms' application and convergence. Together, these analyses connect algorithmic behavior, convergence conditions, and the statistics responsible for learned features.
neurips-1999-algorithms-for-independent-.tldr: A noisy generative model connects ICA algorithms to constrained expectation-maximization and explains the role of higher-order correlations in learned features.

paragraphs: This paper presents a variational Bayesian approach to choosing models within families of kernel classifiers, including support vector machines and Gaussian processes. Kernel parameters determine aspects of the model's representation of the data. Selecting those parameters is therefore part of deciding which classifier is appropriate for a particular learning problem.

The proposed algorithm adapts many kernel parameters without user interaction and without setting aside training examples for validation. This matters especially when choosing among more elaborate kernel families: the method provides a way to fit their parameters while keeping the available cases in the training process. Variational Bayesian inference supplies the framework for that selection.

The authors argue that this capability opens the possibility of using sophisticated kernels when small, standard kernel families are inappropriate. This is a statement about the opportunities the method creates, rather than a universal performance guarantee. The paper also relates the approach to Gaussian-process research and clarifies connections between support vector machines and certain Gaussian-process models.
neurips-1999-bayesian-model-selection-fo.tldr: Variational Bayesian model selection adapts many kernel parameters automatically without holding out training cases for validation.

paragraphs: This paper examines why neurons in primary visual cortex, V1, can respond more strongly to a figure than to its background. Responses can also be elevated along the figure's medial axis, its central internal structure, compared with other interior locations. These effects extend across image regions much larger than an individual V1 cell's receptive field.

That mismatch in spatial scale has motivated explanations involving feedback from higher visual areas. The paper shows how mechanisms within V1 can account for the effects when the figure is small or lies within a certain scale. The scale condition is central: the claim is that local visual processing can explain these observations under those circumstances.

The proposed explanation connects the response patterns to segmentation before attention is directed to the image. These processes detect and emphasize boundaries between regions with relatively uniform visual properties. Figure-ground and medial-axis responses thus become manifestations of the same segmentation processes, providing a V1-based explanation for effects that might otherwise be attributed to higher-area feedback.
neurips-1999-can-vi-mechanisms-account-f.tldr: V1 segmentation mechanisms can explain figure-ground and medial-axis response enhancements for figures within particular size conditions.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how random changes in voltage-gated ion channels produce fluctuations in a neuron's membrane voltage. These channels contribute to the electrical behavior of neural membranes, so their randomness may affect how reliably neurons process information. The study focuses on the relationship between channel kinetics and voltage noise below the threshold for a spike.

The authors use Monte Carlo simulations of a stochastic Markov version of the Mainen-Sejnowski model of dendritic excitability in cortical neurons. Within these simulations, changes that increase excitability, including higher channel densities and lower temperature, also increase the magnitude of subthreshold voltage noise. Noise grows as the membrane moves from its resting voltage toward the firing threshold.

These findings connect increased responsiveness with increased electrical variability in the modeled membrane. The authors suggest that channel fluctuations may interfere with a neuron's ability to integrate synaptic inputs and may constrain the precision and reliability of information processing. That functional consequence is presented as an implication of the simulations, rather than a directly established universal limit.
neurips-1999-channel-noise-in-excitable-.tldr: Simulations link greater membrane excitability to stronger channel-driven voltage noise, suggesting possible limits on reliable neural integration.

paragraphs: This paper studies a Hebbian cell assembly: a group of spiking neurons whose connections change through a timing-dependent learning rule. The rule is motivated by experimental findings. A short delay from a presynaptic spike to a postsynaptic spike strengthens the connection, while spikes occurring in the reverse order weaken it.

The analysis considers the interaction between changing synaptic connections and changing neuronal activity. Connections influence when neurons fire, and spike timing in turn influences the connections. The authors find several possible collective behaviors: neurons can fire asynchronously, synchronize completely, or exhibit what they call distributed synchrony.

In distributed synchrony, the assembly spontaneously separates into groups that fire in a repeating cycle. This provides a form of coordinated activity without requiring every neuron to fire together. The paper investigates that behavior through simulations and analytical calculations of the resulting synaptic distributions. Its contribution is to show how the coupled dynamics of timing-based learning and neural activation can support distinct patterns of coordination within an assembly.
neurips-1999-distributed-synchrony-of-sp.tldr: Timing-dependent synaptic learning can produce assemblies that split spontaneously into groups firing in a repeating cycle.

paragraphs: This paper proposes three simple approximations for computing the posterior mean in Gaussian-process classification. The posterior mean summarizes the model after incorporating observed training data. The focus is on practical ways to calculate this quantity approximately, giving Gaussian-process classifiers alternative computational routes for learning from examples.

Two approaches draw on mean-field ideas from statistical physics. The third uses a Bayesian online approach motivated by results from the statistical mechanics of neural networks. These provide different approximations within the same classification setting, and the paper examines useful consequences of both the mean-field and online perspectives.

The simulations suggest that Bayesian evidence computed through the mean-field approach may help tune hyperparameters, the settings that govern the model. They also suggest that the online approach may reach low training error quickly. These are distinct findings: one concerns selecting model settings, while the other concerns speed of fitting the training examples. The latter claim specifically addresses training error, preserving the scope of the reported result.
neurips-1999-efficient-approaches-to-gau.tldr: Three Gaussian-process classification approximations show potential for evidence-based hyperparameter tuning and rapid reduction of training error.

paragraphs: This paper builds a probability model for images by organizing information across a resolution pyramid. It first shows that any image distribution can be decomposed exactly into conditional distributions of features at one resolution given image information at lower resolutions. This gives a precise way to relate finer image structure to coarser context.

Making the model manageable also calls for factoring computations across spatial positions. The authors identify a problem with that step: it can lose dependencies between distant parts of an image. They introduce hidden class labels at every pyramid pixel to address this issue, producing a hierarchy of mixtures of conditional probabilities with a structure resembling a hidden Markov model on a tree.

The model's parameters can be estimated by maximum likelihood using expectation-maximization. Preliminary applications include detecting objects in synthetic aperture radar images and recognizing targets in optical aerial images. The authors describe these results as encouraging. The contribution combines an exact multiresolution starting point with a structured probabilistic model intended to make image modeling tractable while retaining broader dependencies.
neurips-1999-hierarchical-image-probabil.tldr: A hierarchical image model uses hidden labels across resolution levels to address dependencies lost by simple spatial factorization.

paragraphs: This paper compares image representations for automatically identifying facial actions in image sequences. The target is the Facial Action Coding System, which describes facial movement through component actions and ordinarily requires highly trained human coders. Automating those component labels could support the kinds of behavioral investigations that already use the coding system.

The comparison includes representations learned through principal component analysis, independent component analysis, local feature analysis, and Fisher's linear discriminants. It also includes Gabor wavelets, whose basis images are predefined. The central question is how these different ways of representing facial images affect recognition of the underlying facial actions.

Gabor wavelets and independent component analysis perform best in the reported comparison, each reaching 96% accuracy on 12 facial actions. The independent component representation uses roughly 100 times fewer basis images and requires 90% less CPU time to compute for new images than the Gabor representation. The findings support the usefulness of local image components, high spatial frequencies, and statistical independence for this classification task.
neurips-1999-image-representations-for-f.tldr: ICA and Gabor representations both achieved 96% accuracy on 12 facial actions, with ICA requiring substantially fewer basis images and less computation.

paragraphs: This paper examines a perceptual law in which ratios of choice probabilities separate into two components: one controlled by the stimulus and another controlled by context. Such a pattern has been interpreted as evidence against feedback models of perception. The authors investigate whether that conclusion follows from the observed separation of influences.

They analyze neural-network models described by stochastic differential equations and relate the law to a condition called channel separability. In this condition, processing channels converge on response units without direct lateral connections between channels. Their sensors also avoid direct contamination from external inputs supplied to the other channels.

The analysis finds that the factorization law has little to do with whether feedback connections exist. Instead, the relevant issue is how information channels interact and receive inputs. This changes what the behavioral pattern can establish about an underlying model: a separation of stimulus and context effects points toward channel organization, rather than serving as a general argument against feedback in perception.
neurips-1999-information-factorization-i.tldr: Factorized stimulus and context effects are tied to channel separability and do not generally rule out feedback models of perception.

paragraphs: This paper develops an approach for helping engineers design analog circuits using Markov fields. It represents even highly nonlinear and discontinuous circuit behavior through potential functions based on Kirchhoff's current law. Those functions translate circuit relationships into an objective that a computational procedure can optimize.

The supplied description uses discrete variables with finitely many possible values and a graph that specifies their neighborhood relationships. Potential functions express preferences for combinations of values within connected groups. This representation connects local circuit constraints with an overall design objective. The paper also describes a relatively efficient optimization algorithm and sketches a proof of its convergence.

The empirical example concerns a JFET transistor circuit model. The algorithm selects circuit components that accurately reproduce the desired characteristic curves, demonstrating the approach on a concrete design problem. The paper presents the example as illustrating both strengths and limitations. Its main contribution combines a circuit representation, an optimization method, and evidence that their combination can recover components producing specified electrical behavior.
neurips-1999-kirchoff-law-markov-fields-.tldr: A Markov-field formulation based on Kirchhoff's current law selects components that reproduce desired curves in a JFET circuit model.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the current observation does not provide a complete Markov description of the environment. It uses a dynamic Bayesian network to represent conditional independence among variables compactly. The network's parameters are learned online, so the representation is updated as experience arrives.

The method uses approximations both for inference and for computing the optimal value function. These serve different roles: inference concerns the environment's hidden state, while the value function concerns the desirability of future behavior. The authors investigate how approximations in each part affect the final policy using a moderately difficult driving task.

Linear and quadratic value-function approximations perform similarly on that task, although the quadratic version is more sensitive to initialization. Both remain below human performance. The dynamic Bayesian network achieves performance comparable to a model with a localist hidden-state representation while requiring exponentially fewer parameters. The result supports the compactness of the factored representation without claiming that it solves the task at a human level.
neurips-1999-learning-factored-represent.tldr: A learned dynamic Bayesian network matches a localist model on a driving task with exponentially fewer parameters, while remaining below human performance.

paragraphs: This paper introduces an iterative algorithm for building classifiers called vector machines. It draws together ideas from support vector machines, boosting, and generalized additive models. The goal is a practical classification procedure, and the authors describe the resulting algorithm as simple to implement.

The method can work with several continuously differentiable functions that bound the discrete classification loss, which counts incorrect predictions. These smooth functions provide alternatives to directly optimizing a loss that changes abruptly when a prediction crosses the decision boundary. The paper also presents a norm-penalized version for the exponential loss used in AdaBoost, adding a penalty tied to the size of the learned model.

The authors test two loss functions on synthetic and natural data. On the natural datasets, classification performance is comparable to support vector machines, while runtime is typically shorter. The finding is therefore a reported practical tradeoff: the iterative approach can retain comparable predictive performance in those experiments while often reducing the time needed to obtain it.
neurips-1999-leveraged-vector-machines-4.tldr: An iterative vector-machine algorithm achieves performance comparable to SVMs on natural data while typically running faster.

paragraphs: This paper asks how large a neural network with sigmoidal units must be to approximate continuous functions. Its focus is on lower bounds: establishing required network size rather than constructing a particular approximation algorithm. Such a result concerns the resources that an approximation demands, even before choosing a method for learning the network.

For polynomial approximation, the authors report a required growth scale involving the fourth root of the logarithm of the polynomial degree. They state that the bound applies regardless of input dimension. This makes polynomial degree the explicit complexity quantity in the result, with the bound remaining valid independently of the number of variables.

The proof introduces a method that uses upper bounds on Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension to derive lower bounds on approximation size. It connects a measure of a model family's expressive capacity to the resources needed for continuous-function approximation. The contribution is both a size restriction for sigmoidal networks and a proof strategy for obtaining such restrictions.
neurips-1999-lower-bounds-on-the-complex.tldr: The paper derives lower bounds on sigmoidal-network size for continuous-function approximation using upper bounds on VC dimension.

paragraphs: This paper presents a Monte Carlo approach to learning actions in partially observable environments with real-valued states and actions. Because the true state is not fully visible, the learner works with beliefs about what that state might be. The method therefore has to combine reasoning about uncertainty with learning which actions are valuable.

Importance sampling represents those beliefs, and Monte Carlo approximation propagates them as the process evolves. Value iteration then learns value functions over belief states, making uncertainty part of the decision-making representation. A sample-based nearest-neighbor method generalizes across states, allowing the learning procedure to relate different situations through the available samples.

The contribution is the combination of these sampling and reinforcement-learning components in a method for continuous state and action spaces under partial observation. The authors report initial empirical results suggesting that it works well in practical applications. That wording supports a promising early assessment of the approach, with the evidence framed as initial experience rather than a broad guarantee of practical success.
neurips-1999-monte-carlo-pomdps-b82b4f25.tldr: A sampling-based POMDP algorithm combines belief tracking, value iteration, and nearest-neighbor generalization for real-valued states and actions.

paragraphs: This paper challenges the idea that interesting neural computation necessarily requires several layers of nonlinear units. It proves that a single k-winner-take-all operation applied to weighted input sums can compute any Boolean function. A single soft winner-take-all operation applied to such sums can also approximate any continuous function arbitrarily closely.

The weighted sums require only positive weights. The authors connect this property to biological interest in predominantly excitatory cortical connections and proposed winner-take-all microcircuits. The mathematical point is that selecting among competing linear responses provides enough nonlinearity for universal computational power, even when the preceding weighted sums are restricted in this way.

The paper also argues for winner-take-all as a hardware building block. It cites efficient analog implementations and proves that multilayer perceptrons need a number of gates growing quadratically with the number of inputs to compute winner-take-all. This comparison highlights how choosing the basic computational unit changes circuit complexity: an operation that is compact as a dedicated circuit can be expensive to reproduce using perceptron gates.
neurips-1999-neural-computation-with-win.tldr: Winner-take-all can supply the only nonlinear operation needed for universal neural computation, with positive weights in the preceding linear sums.

paragraphs: This paper asks how wide axonal and dendritic branching structures should be when two neuronal layers connect topographically and have different neuron densities. It treats the problem as one of minimizing the total volume occupied by axons and dendrites. The numbers of outputs reached by each input neuron and inputs received by each output neuron are taken as given.

Under that setup, the author analytically determines the arbor widths that minimize wiring volume. The qualitative rule is that neurons in the sparser layer should have wider arbors than neurons in the denser layer. This relates the spatial extent of neural branches to the density of the populations they connect.

The rule agrees with anatomical data from retinal and cerebellar neurons whose morphology and connectivity are known. The author also suggests that it may help infer connectivity from morphology. That potential application runs the relationship in reverse: observed branching shapes could offer clues about connections, using the volume-minimization framework and its specified connectivity constraints.
neurips-1999-optimal-sizes-of-dendritic-.tldr: Minimizing wiring volume predicts wider neuronal arbors in the sparser of two connected layers, consistent with cited anatomical observations.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with a policy represented by its own function approximator, separately from the value function. The policy parameters are updated in the direction that increases expected reward. This provides a direct way to improve action selection while allowing the policy to choose actions probabilistically.

The motivation includes a difficulty with deriving actions greedily from approximate values: a tiny value change can abruptly switch the selected action. Such discontinuities obstruct convergence analysis. The paper's main result expresses the policy gradient in a form that can be estimated from experience with help from an approximate action-value or advantage function.

Using that result, the authors prove convergence to a locally optimal policy for a version of policy iteration with arbitrary differentiable function approximation. The scope matters: the guarantee concerns the analyzed version of the algorithm and local optimality. The contribution gives direct policy optimization a theoretical foundation while retaining a useful role for approximate value estimates in guiding policy updates.
neurips-1999-policy-gradient-methods-for.tldr: An experience-estimable policy-gradient formula supports a convergence proof to a locally optimal policy for a version of approximate policy iteration.

paragraphs: This paper explores the practical use of reinforcement learning in spoken dialogue systems through a software tool called RLDS. The tool uses a Markov decision process framework, which treats dialogue as a sequence of states and decisions. The authors place the work in the context of substantial technical challenges in applying that framework to real dialogue systems.

They apply RLDS to dialogue corpora collected from two systems built at AT&T Labs. The data contain temporally dependent interactions, so understanding a conversation requires attending to relationships across its sequence. The tool brings the MDP framework to those recorded dialogues as a way to explore their structure.

The experiments indicate promise for browsing complex dialogue corpora and understanding correlations within them. This is the stated practical finding: RLDS can help investigate how aspects of dialogue relate over time. The contribution therefore includes a general software tool and an empirical demonstration of its potential for analysis, with the reported outcome centered on understanding dialogue data.
neurips-1999-reinforcement-learning-for-.tldr: RLDS applies an MDP framework to recorded dialogues and shows promise for exploring correlations across conversation sequences.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for estimating a probability density over several variables from data. Density estimation describes how probability is distributed across possible observations, including which combinations of variable values are more likely. The proposed approach uses the support vector method to formulate the estimation problem.

Specifically, the authors connect density estimation to solving an ill-posed inverse problem and obtain a solution expressed as a mixture of densities. That mixture form represents the estimated distribution by combining component densities. The contribution is a support-vector-based route to determining such an estimate, with Gaussian kernels used in the reported comparisons.

The method compares favorably with Parzen density estimation and Gaussian mixture modeling. On synthetic data, the authors report more accurate density estimates in 2, 6, 12, and 40 dimensions. Those results show the method being evaluated across several dimensionalities, including a substantially multivariate case. The stated evidence concerns estimation accuracy in those synthetic experiments and supports the approach as a useful alternative in the tested settings.
neurips-1999-support-vector-method-for-m.tldr: A support-vector density estimator produces mixture densities and reports improved synthetic-data accuracy over Parzen and Gaussian mixture methods.

paragraphs: This paper adds invariance to image transformations, such as translation and shearing, to generative density models. Such transformations can change an image's appearance without changing the underlying content being modeled. The approach represents transformation as a hidden variable, allowing the probabilistic model to account for multiple transformed versions of an observation.

The key approximation replaces a nonlinear transformation manifold with a discrete collection of transformations. An existing expectation-maximization algorithm can then be extended by taking expectations over that collection. This supplies a concrete mechanism for incorporating transformation uncertainty into learning. The authors show how to apply it to Gaussian mixtures, factor analysis, and mixtures of factor analysers.

Reported applications include filtering microscopy images, clustering faces and facial poses, and modeling and recognizing handwritten digits. These examples demonstrate the range of tasks to which the transformation variable is applied. The methodological contribution is a reusable extension of generative models: transformation handling becomes part of the probabilistic representation and its inference procedure.
neurips-1999-topographic-transformation-.tldr: A discrete hidden transformation variable lets generative image models account for changes such as translation and shearing through extended EM inference.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a boosting algorithm motivated by the behavior of ensembles on noisy classification problems. AdaBoost increasingly concentrates on examples that are hardest to learn. That emphasis can be disadvantageous when some difficult examples are outliers, because improving their treatment may compete with obtaining stronger separation for the other examples.

The authors frame the issue through classification margins, which describe how securely examples sit on the appropriate side of a decision boundary. They emphasize the distribution of margins across the dataset rather than only the smallest margin. The underlying tradeoff is that tolerating some outliers may be worthwhile if it substantially improves margins for the remaining points.

The proposed algorithm permits a prespecified fraction of examples to occupy the margin region or even lie on the incorrect side of the boundary. This builds tolerance for problematic examples into the boosting formulation. The contribution is a method designed around that tradeoff, translating the concern about noisy data into an explicit allowance for a controlled fraction of poorly separated points.
neurips-1999-v-arc-ensemble-learning-in-.tldr: v-Arc modifies boosting to tolerate a prespecified fraction of poorly separated or misclassified examples in pursuit of better margins elsewhere.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian algorithm for learning the structure of a mixture of factor analysers. It can determine both the number of mixture components and the number of factors within each component. Alternatively, it can infer posterior distributions over these choices, retaining uncertainty about the appropriate model structure.

The method uses an efficient, deterministic variational approximation to Bayesian integration over parameters. The authors attribute resistance to overfitting to integrating out those parameters. A stochastic procedure for adding components also permits incremental variational optimization and can help avoid local maxima. In nontrivial synthetic examples, the method correctly identifies the component counts and their dimensionalities.

A further contribution uses importance sampling from the variational approximation to obtain unbiased estimates of the true evidence, exact predictive density, and divergence between approximate and true posteriors. These quantities respectively concern model support, prediction, and approximation quality. The authors present this sampling technique as applicable beyond factor-analyser mixtures to variational approximations more generally.
neurips-1999-variational-inference-for-b.tldr: Variational Bayesian inference learns mixture size and local dimensionality, while importance sampling provides unbiased estimates of key Bayesian quantities.
